title: Trump blasts Newsom’s death penalty commutations as ‘shocking act of injustice’
html:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump blasted Gov. Gavin Newsom’s decision to commute every death sentence in California, calling the move “one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen” at a Monday press conference with victims’ family members at the Department of Justice.

President Donald Trump listens as Sandy Friend speaks about her late son Michael Lyons, at the Department of Justice in Washington on Nov. 23, 2026.

Trump said he “couldn’t believe” Newsom’s choice to commute the sentences of some of California’s most notorious serial killers and rapists.

He used a good portion of the event to describe in great detail some of the murders that landed the 548 condemned people in California on death row, specifically mentioning Charles Ng, who was convicted of murdering nine adults and two children in 1984-85, Randy Kraft, a serial murderer known in the 1970s and ‘80s as the “Scorecard Killer” and Robert Boyd Rhoades, who brutally raped, tortured and killed 8-year-old Michael Lyons in 1996, among others.

“You’d have to read their biographies to see how bad they were. Some of them you wouldn’t even believe,” Trump said, calling Newsom a “terrible governor.”

“He stood with the murderers and the child slayers,” he said. “But today we say the American people stand with you.”

Trump’s press conference seemed designed as much to politically whack Newsom over the commutations as it was to honor victims, representing the latest chapter in the years-long feud between the two men who have regularly sparred during their overlapping time in office over crime and punishment.

Newsom, for his part, said his commutations decision, which he announced earlier this month, was inspired in part by a national reckoning over the death penalty, including a botched execution in Tennessee and a Trump administration announcement — later walked back — that it planned to livestream a federal execution by a firing squad.

Newsom slammed Trump in a video he posted just before the press conference, calling out the president for what he claimed was blatant hypocrisy. He said Trump has used his post to pardon numerous criminals, including those with close ties to the president or his allies. Trump also granted widespread clemency to nearly all of the Jan. 6 defendants, many of whom went on to reoffend.

“Donald Trump doesn’t oppose mercy. He sells it,” Newsom said. “If you are poor, Black or brown, you get the needle. If you are rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call.”

Newsom noted that in 1989, Trump called for the death penalty for the so-called Central Park Five, or the five Black and Latino teenagers who were wrongfully convicted of raping a white woman in the park.

“They were innocent, DNA proved it, you never apologized,” Newsom said.

Both Newsom and Trump have touted crime statistics to promote their agendas and policy priorities. Trump said during the event that “crime rates have gone down 84%,” though it was unclear what specific crimes he was referencing or if it was an overall national or local trend. Newsom’s office has in recent weeks also touted lower crimes in California, including a “record low” homicide rate.

Trump’s event underscores the intense scrutiny and political backlash that has surrounded Newsom since he made his decision, which already faces at least one legal challenge and that in some cases must be reviewed under state law by the California Supreme Court.

But the president’s choice to orchestrate such a major event to publicly admonish a governor’s decision is unusual, said Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of UC Berkeley Law School.

“I do not recall a president ever attempting to undermine a governor’s commuting of death sentences,” Chemerinsky said in an email. “Other governors have done this, but to my knowledge, no president ever has done this before.”

Share your thoughts on Gov. Newsom commuting 548 death sentences

That’s in part because, however controversial, governors have legal jurisdiction over state commutations so Trump has little, if any, power to stop Newsom’s action.

Article continues below this ad

“This is a publicity stunt by the president, not a serious legal effort,” Chemerinsky said.

Several family members of victims also spoke at the event, during which they celebrated Trump and ridiculed Newsom.

“Michael was 8 years old. He loved his sisters, fishing, Ninja Turtles, telling campfire stories and bringing me flowers. Michael was afraid of the dark. He believed the boogeyman was going to get him,” his mother, Sandy Friend said, battling tears.

Friend said the night her son was killed, “Michael learned that the boogeyman was real.”

She said Newsom, with the swipe of a pen and without notifying families, “erased” justice for her son’s killer.

Article continues below this ad

“You took the only justice we had and let families feel abandoned by the state that promised to protect us,” she said. “You’ll never understand the unimaginable pain that you’re putting these families through. Face me, Governor Newsom. Tell me Michael’s life doesn’t matter.”

Newsom was careful to focus his criticism on Trump and did not use the video to explain his decision or undermine victims’ grief. In an open letter to Californians announcing the commutations, Newsom said he agonized over it for years and ultimately made his choice over a firm belief that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values.”

He also told the Chronicle in an interview earlier this month that he made the choice after speaking with the sisters of Polly Klaas, a 12-year-old who was abducted from her home in Petaluma in 1993 and brutally killed. The man convicted of murdering her was sentenced to death and is still alive.

“This decision was not made by a jury. It was not approved by the voters. It was made by one politician acting alone,” Marc Klaas, Polly’s father, said at the event. “While nothing can bring Polly back, her life mattered. The pain inflicted on our family was real.”

Newsom acknowledged the families who joined Trump’s press conference to denounce the commutations in his Monday video.

“To the families standing with him today, your grief is real,” he said. “That’s why every person, every person, on California’s former death row will die in prison. No one walks out. Donald Trump’s criminals? They walk out.”

Speculation had swirled for weeks that Newsom would commute the sentences before he leaves office in January and before launching an expected 2028 presidential bid. The decision could help Newsom earn support from the more progressive wing of his party in what’s expected to be a crowded Democratic primary field, but it could also hobble his odds against more law-and-order candidates who appeal to anti-MAGA Republicans and swing voters.

The White House emphasized that California voters have repeatedly rejected efforts to overturn the death penalty, including as early as 2016, when they voted against a ballot measure to ban it and passed another to speed up executions, part of which was later invalidated by the courts.

National support for the death penalty also remains strong. A July 2026 survey by the Pew Research Center found that two-thirds of American adults support capital punishment for people convicted of murder, including 51% of Democrats and 84% of Republicans.

Trump touted an executive order he signed on his first day back in office “restoring the death penalty” after former President Joe Biden commuted the sentences of 37 people on federal death row during his last days in office.

Trump also announced Monday he would sign a directive “ordering the Department of Justice to seek the death penalty for child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims,” adding that the order would also “expedite the execution of federal death sentences.”

It’s unclear how or whether the order would affect California and Newsom’s commutations, which are within his jurisdiction as governor. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for clarification.

Trump also said Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, would introduce a bill to “strengthen the death penalty in America.”

“And it’s going to be much different than it was in the past,” Trump said. “It’s going to be strong and it’ll be swift.”

Natasha Minsker, a lobbyist who has worked with a coalition of anti-death penalty advocates urging Newsom to commute the sentences, slammed Trump for using the death penalty for “political purposes” in a way that doesn’t help victims or their families.

“It is once again prosecutors and politicians using the death penalties to bring attention to themselves and for their own political gain and with no eye to what’s in the best interest of the families and with no interest to what actually protects our communities and keeps us safe,” she said. “This is a state law issue. This is about whether people in California support the governor, and it’s about the governor’s ability to commute under the state Constitution.”
summary: President Trump dwelled on gruesome details of several murders and condemned California’s governor during an event at the Department of Justice with victims’ families.
